newsitem.title: USA: Strong dlr seen a drag on US economy through 1998.
newsitem.headline: Strong dlr seen a drag on US economy through 1998.

text.p: The dollar's continuing rally will restrain the U.S. economy well into 1998, easing the need for the Federal Reserve to hike official interest rates, experts said.
U.S. economic growth is currently influenced by the dollar's value more than at any time since World War II, given the burgeoning share of the U.S. economy represented by trade.

Exports jumped to nearly 12 percent of U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 from below seven percent in 1986. That remains a small piece compared with most U.S. trading partners, where trade accounts for a third or more of GDP. But analysts said global competition makes trade a key to U.S. economic growth.

"It is true to say that 30 years ago, the American economy could ignore what was going on abroad, because exports were four percent of GDP," said Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc. "Now, we're becoming more sensitive to exchange rates."

The dollar has surged 55 percent against the yen and 25 percent against the mark from lows in early 1995. On Thursday, the dollar stood at 124.10 yen and 1.6830 marks -- up from 117 yen and 1.59 marks just a month ago.
Economists noted that a rising dollar is a double-edged sword. It restrains inflation by making imported goods less expensive but hinders growth by making exports more expensive.
As a result, "it could be the Fed can wait longer to tighten, and when they do tighten, they don't have to tighten as much," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.

The five percent rise in the trade-weighted value of the dollar since last fall is roughly equivalent to a 50-basis -point increase in the federal funds rate, according to St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers LLC -- formerly Laurence Meyer & Associates. And analysts pointed out an interest rate hike would boost the dollar still higher.

"If the Fed had previously concluded that a 50-basis-point increase in the fed funds rate was necessary to achieve its growth and inflation targets, and other factors remained unchanged except for the appreciation of the dollar, the Fed could sit out and allow the exchange rate to do the work that the rate increase would have," said Chris Vavares, economist and president of Macroeconomic Advisers.
Citing an 18-month to two-year lag beween big changes in the dollar's value and their economic effect, economists said the dollar should remain a drag on the economy through 1998.
Vavares calculated that the five-percent appreciation in the trade-weighed dollar reduces GDP by 0.3 percent after four quarters and 0.8 percent after eight quarters.
Therefore, "we haven't yet to feel the impact of the rising dollar since the spring of 1995," Shepherdson said.

"If anything, at the end of (1996) exports were still benefitting from the fall of the dollar in 1994," he said. "The impact of the dollar's strength won't start hurting until mid-year," he said, adding it "will hurt significantly."

Shephersdon said a five percent appreciation in the trade-weighted value of the dollar is equal to about a 100 basis-point rise in the fed funds rate. Still, he called a U.S. recession unlikely. He said he would not rule out a tightening by the Fed, although he said one is not imminent.

Experts generally agreed the dollar has hit a ceiling. They expect the dollar to slip in the near future, but remain strong enough so less vigorous exports act as a drag on U.S. growth, while prices for imports stay low.

Import prices excluding petroleum are about 1.7 percent lower than a year ago, noted Steven Wieting, associate economist at Smith Barney Inc. "Since July, import prices have been down 1.5 percent or more year over year in every month," he said. "And they have been lower than year-earlier levels in every month since May."

Wieting said that for every one percent monthly increase in the trade-weighted dollar value, import prices fall 0.1 to 0.2 percent a month. Economists also said U.S. firms have generally held down their own prices to stay competitive.
The Labor Department on Friday reported a 0.3-percent fall in the producer price index in January -- its first decline since October, 1994.
There are some skeptics who dispute the dollar's strength.

"The dollar's gains versus the yen and D-mark overstate the magnitude of the dollar's gains," said John Praveen, economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. Praveen said Merrill's trade-weighted index shows less impressive dollar gains than others. In 1996, he said, on an export-weighted basis it was up three percent and up four percent on an import-weighted basis. So far in 1997, he said the dollar is up two percent on an export-weighted basis and 2.5 percent on an import-weighted basis.
He also noted the dollar has fallen against the British pound and Canadian dollar in 1997.

Robert Mellman, economist at J.P. Morgan & Co. said he doubted U.S. export growth would be hurt since the U.S. trades more with Canada and Mexico than Japan and Germany. He said the dollar's recent rise compares to a 50 to 75 basis point tightening, which he believes would not keep the economy from growing above its potential.
"The trend of exports will be stronger, not weaker," Mellman said. So, "the pressure is still on the Fed. Whether they move in March or put off the tightening a meeting (until May) is hard to say."
As far as low import prices, he said they have no impact on service sector prices, which are still rising.
"The strong dollar has definitely been a positive in keeping inflation down," Mellman said. "But the inflation threat is from the labor market, and growth from labor continues."
